name: The Law of Large Numbers
statement: Run a random process enough times and the average settles on the true mean.
meaning: The law of large numbers says that as the number of independent trials of a random process grows, the average of the results converges to the expected value, the true underlying mean. Flip a fair coin enough times and the fraction of heads approaches one-half. The long-run average stabilises, provided that mean exists.
mechanism: Averaging dilutes randomness. For independent observations each with the same variance, the variance of their average is that variance divided by the number of observations, which shrinks toward zero as the count grows. So the average concentrates ever more tightly around the mean. There are two forms differing in how strongly they say this: the weak law, that the average is very likely close to the mean for large samples, and the strong law, that the sequence of averages converges to the mean with probability one.

examples.text: The proportion of heads in many flips approaches one-half, even though the absolute gap between the counts of heads and tails tends to grow rather than shrink.
A casino may lose a single spin, but over millions of bets its realised profit converges to the mathematical house edge — the law of large numbers made into a business model, as in insurance.
Estimating a quantity by averaging over many random trials works precisely because the average converges to the true expected value as the number of trials grows.

variants.name: The weak and strong laws
variants.text: The weak law gives convergence in probability, that the average is likely near the mean; the strong law gives almost-sure convergence, that the averages themselves converge to the mean with probability one.

variants.name: The law of averages
variants.text: The folk version, which correctly senses that long-run frequencies reflect probabilities but wrongly assumes a short-term balancing must occur — the root of the gambler's fallacy.

whyItMatters: It is the mathematical guarantee that makes statistics, gambling houses, insurance, and simulation work — the assurance that averages over many trials are predictable even when single outcomes are not. It is the bridge between probability as a theoretical measure and the observed frequencies of the real world, and one of the oldest theorems of the field.

working.text: expect the average of many independent trials to approach the mean, while saying nothing about any single outcome.
increase the number of observations to shrink the variance of the average and pin down the true mean.
do not expect past outcomes to be corrected; convergence comes from diluting early deviations, not from compensating for them.

limits: The law requires a finite expected value: for a distribution with no mean, such as the Cauchy, the average of many draws does not converge, having the same distribution as a single one. It requires independence, or suitable conditions, and bounded variance in the simplest forms. And it is about averages, not individual outcomes — even as the proportion of heads approaches one-half, the absolute difference between the counts of heads and tails almost surely grows large as the flips accumulate.
misreadings: The law does not mean short-run deviations get corrected — after a run of heads, tails is not more likely, since a fair coin has no memory. The average converges by dilution, as more trials divide early deviations by an ever-larger number, not by later outcomes compensating for earlier ones. Believing otherwise is the gambler's fallacy, the mistaken folk law of averages.
origin: First proved by Jacob Bernoulli for the binomial case in his 'Ars Conjectandi' (1713), his golden theorem; named the law of large numbers by Poisson in 1837, with the weak law refined by Chebyshev and Khinchin and the strong law established by Borel and Kolmogorov.
